messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Nguyen was seventy-six, a mechanic who had run her own small garage for forty years, and she had never been afraid of much until the stalking began. It started with a customer—a man whose truck she had repaired twice—who began waiting outside the garage at closing time, standing in the dirt patch beside the bay door where the smell of rain-soaked earth clung to his boots. At first she assumed he was just early for an appointment, but he followed her home, parked down the street, and eventually began leaving notes under the windshield of her old sedan. The police were called, a restraining order was filed, and he disappeared after a few months, but the damage was already done. Now, two years later, Linh could not explain what had happened without losing the thread of her own story—she would start describing the dirt and his shadow, then the sentences would tangle, and she would give up. The memory existed instead as a series of perfect photographs in her mind: the way he stood with his hands in his pockets, the grain of the soil beneath his shoes, the exact angle of the evening light. But if she tried to hold one of those images for more than a second, her mind slammed a door on it before the picture could fully form.

The smell of soil was the worst trigger. Even now, when she walked from her garage to the parts supplier and passed a freshly turned garden bed, the scent would hit her nostrils and the photographic memory would snap open—the man, the dirt, the waiting—and she would feel her chest tighten. Stress did the same thing: a rush of work orders, a tight deadline, and the intrusive images would surface without warning. And what frightened her most was that feeling happy could also bring it back. A moment of relaxation, a laugh with a customer, and then suddenly the memory would intrude, as if her own contentment was a trap. She had come to believe that any moment of peace was dangerous, that pleasure itself signaled threat, and so she stayed taut, scanning, ready.

Linh had become hypervigilant in ways that exhausted her. She checked behind her constantly, even on the short walk from her house to the garage, her head swiveling to confirm no one was following. She was superalert and on guard, and the vigilance itself triggered more memories—a glance over her shoulder would summon the photographic image of the man behind her, and then she would be back in the fear. That fear made her hypersensitive to triggers: the more alert she was, the more she noticed the smell of soil on her own hands after wiping a greasy part, or the way stress buzzed in her ears, or the fleeting warmth of an unexpected happy moment. Each trigger looped back into a memory, and each memory kept her on guard.

At home, a place that should have been safe, Linh felt just as watchful. She checked the locks three times before bed, and she had stopped sitting in the armchair that faced the backyard because the scent of the neighbor's compost pile drifted in through the window. Her husband, a retired postal carrier, had learned not to surprise her from behind; she would flinch and snap, then feel ashamed. The avoidance had shaped her days: she worked longer hours at the garage to avoid the quiet evening hours, and she had stopped accepting help from unfamiliar customers, turning away work to keep strangers out of her bay. The isolation was wearing on her marriage, and her husband had gently suggested she talk to someone.

What finally brought Linh to the clinic was a morning when she walked into her garage and caught the faint smell of soil from a potted plant a customer had left on the counter. The photographic memory seized her—the man, the dirt, the waiting—and she could not move for several minutes. She had to sit down. She realized, staring at her trembling hands, that she was living inside a loop she could not break on her own. She was afraid of what the memories would do to her if she stayed this vigilant forever. But she was also terrified that letting the guard down would invite him back, even though she knew, logically, that he was gone. She came seeking help, she said, because she wanted to sleep through the night without the photographs, and because she wanted to feel the rain without the fear.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly influences or increases triggers; the causal link is mediated by threat/hypervigilance.
